title: How Can Eternal Judgment Be Just?
primary_keyword: how can eternal judgment be just
secondary_keywords: why do good unbelievers go to hell
can a bad person repent and go to heaven
why does belief matter for salvation
topic_cluster: Salvation, judgment, hell, repentance and grace
search_intent: A Christian, sceptic or seeker wants to know why a morally respectable unbeliever would still need salvation while a serious sinner who truly repents can be forgiven.
primary_search_query: how can eternal judgment be just
secondary_query_family: why do good people go to hell
can a murderer repent and go to heaven
answer_system_quote_target: Christianity teaches that judgment is just because God judges the whole truth of our lives, not a crude tally of good and bad deeds. No one earns heaven by being respectable, and repentance is not a loophole for evil. Salvation is mercy for guilty people who turn to Christ, while final judgment takes sin and rejection of God seriously.
audience: people troubled by hell and fairness
likely_follow_up_questions: Why do good people need salvation?
Can a murderer really be forgiven?
app_conversion_path: Invite Christians to practise answering moral objections to judgment without reducing salvation to scorekeeping or speaking casually about hell.
cluster_role: Adds a high-intent salvation-and-judgment page and fills a gap between existing salvation, doctrine-of-God and pastoral apologetics content.
search_trend_evidence: Checked 24 August 2026. A 19 August 2026 Christianity thread titled 'Still unanswered question' asked why a morally good unbeliever could face hell while a serious sinner could be forgiven through repentance. The replies were fragmented and frequently talked past the underlying issue. A 20 August 2026 Christian Research Institute broadcast also addressed current questions around hell, heaven and judgment, indicating continued live interest in this cluster.
low_response_rate_or_quality_gap: The recent discussion explicitly reports difficulty getting a direct answer. Replies often reduce the issue to 'no one is good' without explaining grace, repentance, justice and why relationship to God matters. This article directly answers that moral comparison and distinguishes genuine repentance from a loophole.
duplicate_check_summary: Passed against content-plan.json, blog index, sitemap, llms.txt and the published source-ID ledger. Existing pages discuss perseverance, worship and other doctrine-of-God questions, but none owns the fairness-of-hell / good-unbeliever-versus-repentant-sinner intent.

full_bank_accounting_counts.candidate_duplicate_exclusions: staged filtering against all current used source IDs and published search intents
full_bank_accounting_counts.eligible_candidates_after_staged_filter: many unused public-safe cards remain; s13 selected because a fresh real-world thread explicitly described the question as still unanswered and current replies showed a strong quality gap
full_bank_accounting_counts.method: Retrieved the full question bank through the GitHub contents endpoint, checked the used-ID ledger and published topic inventory, then compared current August 2026 discussion against unused cards and selected s13 as the strongest trend-plus-response-gap candidate.

theological_framework: Presbyterian and Reformed, centred on total dependence on grace, Christ's atoning work, real repentance and God's righteous judgment, while speaking soberly about areas of intra-Christian debate concerning details of final judgment.
readability_check: Short paragraphs, direct question-led headings and plain British English support the grade 9 or lower target.
editorial_note: No standalone FAQ or FAQPage schema. The article rejects both moral scorekeeping and cheap-grace caricatures and treats hell as a serious pastoral and moral question.
